notes.definition: Risk factors are aspects of a person's lifestyle, or substances in the body or environment, that are linked to an increased rate of a disease. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not for others.
explanation: A risk factor does not mean a person will definitely get a disease; it means that the disease is more common among people with that factor. Risk factors can be lifestyle choices (such as diet, smoking, exercise and alcohol), substances in the body (such as high blood cholesterol) or substances in the environment (such as carcinogens and ionising radiation). Many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors, including genetic ones.

Scientists first find a correlation, for example on a scatter graph, showing that as one factor increases so does the rate of disease. A correlation does not prove that one causes the other. A causal mechanism is proven only when scientists find how the factor causes the disease: for example, chemicals in tobacco smoke are known to damage DNA in lung cells, so smoking is proven to cause lung cancer.

Cardiovascular disease is affected by diet, smoking and exercise. A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, increasing fatty deposits in arteries. Smoking damages artery walls and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by the blood, and nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure. Regular exercise lowers blood pressure and cholesterol and helps maintain a healthy weight, reducing the risk. Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes, in which body cells no longer respond properly to insulin.

Alcohol affects liver and brain function. The liver breaks down alcohol, and long-term heavy drinking can cause liver damage such as cirrhosis. Alcohol slows the brain's reactions and long-term use can cause brain damage. Smoking causes lung diseases such as chronic bronchitis and emphysema, and tar in tobacco smoke contains carcinogens that cause lung cancer. Smoking during pregnancy reduces the oxygen reaching the fetus, causing lower birth weight and premature birth. Alcohol in pregnancy can damage the developing baby's brain and organs (fetal alcohol syndrome).

Carcinogens, including ionising radiation (for example X-rays, gamma rays and radon gas), are risk factors for cancer because they can damage DNA and cause mutations that lead to uncontrolled cell division. UV radiation from the Sun and sunbeds is a risk factor for skin cancer.

Non-communicable diseases have large human and financial costs. The human cost includes illness, reduced quality of life and early death, affecting individuals and their families. Financial costs include treatment by the health service, care, and lost income and productivity when people cannot work. These costs apply at local level (families and communities), national level (health services and the economy) and global level, where the number of people affected is rising and poorer countries may struggle to afford treatment.
keyFacts: A risk factor is linked to an increased rate of a disease.
Risk factors can be lifestyle factors or substances in the body or environment.
Correlation does not prove causation; a causal mechanism must be found.
Diet, smoking and lack of exercise increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.
Alcohol affects liver and brain function.
Smoking causes lung disease and lung cancer.
Smoking and alcohol during pregnancy can harm unborn babies.
Carcinogens, including ionising radiation, are risk factors for cancer.
Many diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors.
Non-communicable diseases have human and financial costs at local, national and global levels.

keyTerms.definition: An aspect of lifestyle, or a substance in the body or environment, linked to an increased rate of a disease.
A relationship between two variables in which they change together.
An explanation of how a factor directly causes a disease.
A substance or type of radiation that can cause cancer.
Radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays that can damage DNA and is a risk factor for cancer.
Being very overweight, with excess body fat; a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.
Scarring and permanent damage of the liver, often caused by long-term heavy alcohol use.
Disease of the heart or blood vessels, such as coronary heart disease.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: Interpreting a scatter graph
workedExamples.question: Describe the relationship shown by the example scatter graph of cigarettes smoked per day against lung cancer deaths.
steps: Look at the general trend: as cigarettes per day increase, deaths per 100 000 increase.
Use data: at 10 cigarettes per day about 30 deaths per 100 000; at 40 per day about 118.
State the limit: a correlation alone does not prove causation, but for smoking a causal mechanism has been found.
workedExamples.answer: Positive correlation: more cigarettes per day, higher lung cancer death rate (about 4 times higher at 40 per day than at 10 per day).

workedExamples.title: Calculating risk
workedExamples.question: In a study, 12 out of 400 non-smokers and 54 out of 600 smokers developed a lung disease. How many times greater is the risk for smokers?

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a correlation proves that one factor causes a disease.
misconceptions.right: In fact a correlation only shows a link; a causal mechanism must be found to prove causation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think having a risk factor means you will definitely get the disease.
misconceptions.right: In fact a risk factor only increases the likelihood; many people with risk factors never develop the disease.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think non-communicable diseases are caused by one single factor.
misconceptions.right: In fact many are caused by the interaction of several factors, such as genes, diet and exercise.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think obesity causes Type 1 diabetes.
misconceptions.right: In fact obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes. Type 1 diabetes is caused by the pancreas not producing enough insulin and is not linked to obesity.

realWorld: UK packets of cigarettes carry health warnings because smoking is proven to cause lung cancer and heart disease.
Pregnant women are advised not to drink alcohol or smoke to protect the developing baby.
Radon gas testing is offered in parts of the UK where granite rocks release this radioactive gas into homes.
Treating Type 2 diabetes and its complications costs the NHS billions of pounds each year.
examTips: When describing a scatter graph, name the type of correlation and quote data from the graph.
Always add that correlation does not prove causation unless a mechanism is known.
Match each risk factor to the specific disease the specification links it to (obesity with Type 2 diabetes; alcohol with liver and brain; smoking with lung disease and cancer).
For cost questions, cover both human and financial costs, and mention local, national and global levels if asked.
summary: Risk factors increase the rate of a disease but do not guarantee it.
Some risk factors have a proven causal mechanism; others only a correlation.
Diet, smoking and exercise affect cardiovascular disease.
Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes; alcohol affects liver and brain.
Smoking causes lung disease and cancer; smoking and alcohol harm unborn babies.
Carcinogens and ionising radiation are cancer risk factors.
Non-communicable diseases have human and financial costs at all levels.

questions.explanation: Obesity is the risk factor linked to Type 2 diabetes in the specification.

questions.question:
Long-term heavy drinking of alcohol damages some organs.
Which organ is most damaged by long-term heavy drinking of alcohol?
questions.explanation: The liver breaks down alcohol and can be permanently damaged (cirrhosis). Alcohol also affects the brain.

questions.question: Which of these is a carcinogen?
questions.explanation: Ionising radiation can damage DNA, causing cancer.

A pathogen that spreads a disease
A treatment that reduces the chance of disease
Something linked to an increased rate of a disease
questions.explanation: A risk factor increases the likelihood of a disease, but does not guarantee it.

questions.question:
Smoking during pregnancy can cause a baby to have a low birth weight.
What is the reason for this?
options: Nicotine is a food for the fetus
Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried by the mother's blood to the fetus
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the fetus and growth slows.

questions.question: Which effect of alcohol on the brain is most likely?
options: Slower reaction times and impaired judgement
questions.explanation: Alcohol is a depressant that slows brain function and reactions.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the sales of ice cream and the number of new cases of skin cancer in a town in different months of one year.
There is a strong positive correlation between the two sets of data.
What is the best explanation for this correlation?

headers: Number of new cases of skin cancer

options: Skin cancer makes people eat more ice cream
Both increase with a third factor, sunny weather and UV exposure
The correlation proves a causal link
questions.explanation: A third factor (sunshine) causes both. This shows why correlation does not prove causation.

questions.question:
Smoking is accepted as a cause of lung cancer, not just as being correlated with it.
Which statement best explains why?
options: Scientists have identified carcinogens in tobacco smoke that damage DNA in lung cells
Lung cancer only occurs in smokers
Smoking is illegal in many places
questions.explanation: A causal mechanism has been found. Not all smokers get lung cancer, and some non-smokers do.

questions.question:
A person has a family history of heart disease.
The person is overweight, smokes and rarely exercises.
Which statement about this person is correct?
options: Only their genes affect their risk
Stopping smoking will have no effect because of their genes
They will definitely have a heart attack
Their risk is increased by the interaction of several genetic and lifestyle factors
questions.explanation: Many diseases result from interacting factors. Changing lifestyle factors can lower overall risk.

questions.explanation: Because both groups are the same size, compare the numbers directly: 63 ÷ 9 = 7 times greater.

Calculate how many times greater the rate of cardiovascular disease was in group B than in group A.

headers: Number of cases of cardiovascular disease

questions.explanation: Group A has more cases but a much larger group. Comparing rates shows group B's rate is 3.2 times greater.

questions.question: Give two effects of smoking on health.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: lung cancer; lung diseases such as bronchitis or emphysema; cardiovascular disease; low birth weight / premature babies if smoking during pregnancy
questions.explanation: Smoking affects the lungs, the circulatory system and unborn babies.

questions.question: Name a disease for which obesity is a risk factor.
questions.explanation: Obesity is linked to Type 2 diabetes in the specification (also cardiovascular disease).

questions.question: Explain how a diet high in saturated fat increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
markScheme: 1 mark: increases blood cholesterol / fatty material deposited in coronary arteries
1 mark: arteries narrow, so less blood and oxygen reach the heart muscle
questions.explanation: Diet links to CHD through cholesterol and fatty deposits in the coronary arteries.

questions.question: Explain why ionising radiation is a risk factor for cancer.
markScheme: 1 mark: ionising radiation damages DNA / causes mutations
1 mark: which can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and division
questions.explanation: Cancer results from changes in cells leading to uncontrolled division; ionising radiation can cause these changes.

questions.question: Describe the human and financial costs of non-communicable diseases.
markScheme: 1 mark: human cost: illness, pain, reduced quality of life or early death
1 mark: effects on families and carers
1 mark: financial cost: cost of treatment and care to health services / lost income or productivity when people cannot work
questions.explanation: Both human and financial costs are needed for full marks.

markScheme: 1 mark: correlation does not prove causation
1 mark: other factors could explain both, such as income, amount of exercise or diet at home
1 mark: a causal mechanism would need to be shown / controlled study needed
questions.explanation: Areas with many outlets may differ in many other ways. Only a controlled study or a known mechanism shows causation.

questions.question: Suggest why the global cost of non-communicable diseases is increasing.
markScheme: 1 mark: populations are growing and ageing / more people living longer
1 mark: more people with risk factors such as obesity or smoking in developing countries / more expensive treatments
questions.explanation: More people with risk factors and longer lives mean more cases needing long-term treatment.

questions.question: Give two ways a person could reduce their risk of cardiovascular disease.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: stop smoking; exercise regularly; eat less saturated fat / balanced diet; lose weight; reduce alcohol intake
questions.explanation: These reduce cholesterol, blood pressure and damage to arteries.

questions.question: Which of these is not a lifestyle risk factor?
questions.explanation: Genes are inherited, not a lifestyle choice, although they can still be a risk factor.

questions.question: Why are pregnant women advised not to drink alcohol?
options: Alcohol can damage the developing baby's brain and organs
Alcohol causes the baby to become obese
Alcohol increases the oxygen supply to the fetus
questions.explanation: Alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause fetal alcohol syndrome.

questions.question: Describe how smoking and drinking alcohol can affect health, including the health of unborn babies.
markScheme: Indicative content: smoking: tar contains carcinogens causing lung cancer; lung diseases such as bronchitis and emphysema; increases risk of cardiovascular disease (damage to arteries, raised blood pressure, carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried). Alcohol: liver damage (cirrhosis); affects brain function, slows reactions, long-term brain damage. Unborn babies: smoking reduces oxygen to the fetus, low birth weight, premature birth; alcohol damages brain and organs (fetal alcohol syndrome).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of effects of both smoking and alcohol, including effects on unborn babies.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some effects of smoking or alcohol given, with limited detail.
questions.explanation: Cover smoking, alcohol and pregnancy for Level 2.

questions.question: Scientists suggested that a high-sugar diet is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes. Explain how scientists could investigate this link, and evaluate the difference between showing a correlation and proving a causal mechanism. Include the human and financial reasons why this research is important.
markScheme: Indicative content: large, representative sample; record sugar intake (diet questionnaire) and whether people develop Type 2 diabetes over time; control or record other factors such as obesity, exercise, age, family history; plot data or compare rates; a correlation shows a link only; other factors such as obesity could explain both; causal mechanism requires evidence of how sugar affects the body (for example weight gain leading to cells not responding to insulin); experimental or long-term studies, repeated by other scientists, peer review; importance: Type 2 diabetes reduces quality of life, causes complications such as blindness and amputation, early death; financial cost to health services of treatment and complications, lost productivity; costs at local, national and global levels; findings could guide public health advice or policy.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): well-planned investigation with control of variables, clear explanation of correlation versus causation, and relevant human and financial costs.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some valid planning points and reference to correlation not proving causation, with some costs.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about the link or costs.
questions.explanation: Top answers show why other variables must be controlled, explain what extra evidence proves causation, and link to costs.
